prize_parts.citation: For the discovery that liquid-liquid phase separation organises the interior of living cells into membraneless compartments
For the development of base editing, programmable chemical conversion of DNA bases without double-strand cleavage

statement.case_for: Phase separation is the one candidate on the shortlist that is a new concept of molecular organisation: cells use thermodynamic phase behaviour, multivalency and polymer physics to create compartments without membranes. It transfers the language of phase diagrams, binodals and material properties into cell biology, and it ties to my own field through amyloid-type aggregation and lipid-protein co-assembly. The 2009 P-granule work of Hyman and Brangwynne is the founding observation, and the concept has been tested in many laboratories. Pairing it with base editing gives a prize with two distinct achievements, one conceptual and one methodological, each with a clean chemical core. Base editing has the broadest opening support (five top-three rankings) and a clear originator in Liu, so this configuration lets the committee honour physical chemistry of life and an enabling chemical tool together.
statement.case_against: The cost of this configuration is Rosen, whose 2012 multivalent-interaction work gave the reconstituted, quantitative chemical basis for phase separation, and Pappu and Mittag, who supplied sequence grammar. Leaving out Rosen is hard to justify on science alone, and it is forced only by the three-person limit once Liu is included. Phase separation is also the least settled on maturity: which cellular condensates are real equilibrium phases, and how much function depends on this, is still contested. Base editing is recent, overlaps with the 2020 CRISPR prize, and a Liu-only credit sets aside Komor, Gaudelli, Kondo and Nishida. A two-part prize of such different topics may read as a compromise.

responses.point: Linke ranks phase separation fourth and values the Hyman-Brangwynne-Rosen triad, but he warns that interpretation is not yet stable because there is strong debate over which cellular structures are truly phase separated.
responses.response: The concern is fair and I share part of it: I would not claim that every reported condensate is an equilibrium phase. But the committee need not rule on that. The citation can rest on the demonstrated, reproducible fact that liquid-like phase separation of proteins and RNA occurs in vitro and in cells and organises them. Physical chemists contest the thermodynamic labelling of individual condensates, which is the normal sign of a vigorous field rather than an unstable one. That is why I credit Hyman and Brangwynne for the founding observation and keep the wording at the level of the concept.

responses.point: Aqvist ranks base editing first as a game-changing tool with clear originators Liu, Komor and Gaudelli, and places phase separation fourth because of its quantitative physical basis but unsettled breadth.
responses.response: I agree that base editing is chemically elegant and mature enough, and it is why I add it to my configuration rather than ignore it. Where I differ is on credit. Komor and Gaudelli were the lead experimentalists, but the prize logic is usually the intellectual driver, and with three slots a Liu-centred credit is the cleanest. I would resist giving base editing the whole prize, because it extends a tool recognised in 2020, whereas phase separation opens a different conceptual area. Johan's quantitative view should push us to ask for evidence on off-target and bystander editing before the final ballot.

responses.point: Aili ranks targeted protein degradation first as a new modality that recruits an E3 ligase to remove undruggable targets, with Crews, Deshaies and Ciulli as the core.
responses.response: I take degraders seriously; it was my fifth choice rather than a dismissal. The design logic of ternary-complex cooperativity is real chemistry. My reservations are timing and attribution: no degrader drug is yet approved, and the PROTAC and molecular-glue strands (Handa, Ito, Gray) have competing claims that the three-person limit cannot separate. I would be more willing to move it up if colleagues can show how the credit divides. As it stands it is my first alternative, not my preferred part.

responses.point: Chabes ranks degraders first and base editing second, proposing Liu alone as the cleanest and least contested configuration, and values measurement quality.
responses.response: A single-name credit for base editing is workable and I am content with Liu alone for that part. I would add that the same demand for quantification applies to phase separation: Rosen's in vitro work is the most quantitative part of the field, which is why leaving him out troubles me. If the committee prefers a single-part prize, I would rather give the whole of B065 to Hyman, Brangwynne and Rosen than split the base-editing credit among the trainees.

uncertainties: Whether the committee sees phase separation as chemistry or cell biology, and whether its maturity is sufficient given the debate over condensate thermodynamics.
Whether Rosen should replace Brangwynne or Liu in the three-person union, or whether a single-part B065 prize with Hyman, Brangwynne and Rosen is better.
How far base editing is distinct from the 2020 CRISPR prize, and the priority record of Kondo and Nishida.
I am relying on memory of the literature and have not verified the credit record or the current clinical status.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for the shortlisted candidates. My research on lipid self-assembly and lipid-protein co-assembly in amyloid is close to the phase-separation field, but this is a scientific proximity, not a personal or institutional tie to any named candidate. B018 (lipid nanoparticles) is also close to my own field, so I will state that as a disclosure if it is discussed further.
